Keeping the Franka Emika Panda alive: a ROS 2 stack
with a reliable position interface

Antonio Langella , Davide Risi , Vincenzo Petrone , Enrico Ferrentino , and Pasquale Chiacchio
Department of Information Engineering, Electrical Engineering, and Applied Mathematics (DIEM), University of Salerno, 84084 Fisciano, Italy
{alangella, drisi, vipetrone, eferrentino, pchiacchio}@unisa.it ††thanks: ˜https://orcid.org/0009-0009-7656-8325††thanks: ˜https://orcid.org/0009-0001-3077-5371††thanks: ˜https://orcid.org/0000-0003-4777-1761††thanks: ˜https://orcid.org/0000-0003-0768-8541††thanks: ˜https://orcid.org/0000-0003-3385-8866
Abstract

This paper presents an open-source software stack that restores ROS 2 support for the Franka Emika Panda robot while resolving the long-standing unreliability of its external position control interface. We first analyze the root causes of unstable position control and show that the observed vibrations and protective stops arise from the timing of the external control loop and sampling jitter, rather than from limitations of the robot itself. Building on this analysis, we introduce an asynchronous hardware interface that decouples real-time communication from the ROS 2 control loop, a rate-matching mechanism for slower command sources, and a position-domain reference generation strategy that produces reliable, smooth position commands. Experimental validation shows that the proposed architecture reliably tracks velocity references by reducing motion artifacts introduced by the official implementation, and the stack is validated across motion planning, compliance control, position-controlled manipulation, and haptic teleoperation on two independent Panda platforms. By restoring a modern, reliable, and open ROS 2 ecosystem for the Panda, this work lowers the barrier to developing safe, responsive, and reproducible human-robot collaboration applications that integrate planning, perception, interaction, and shared autonomy. Code and videos are available on our website at https://sites.google.com/view/fer-ros2/.

1 INTRODUCTION

The Franka Emika Robot (FER), widely known in the community as the Franka Emika Panda (Panda, in the following), is one of the most common platforms for manipulation research and collaborative robotics [Haddadin et al., 2022]. Its torque-controlled arm, force sensitivity and open control interface made it a de-facto standard in academic laboratories, where a large installed base is still in daily use [Daniel et al., 2024, de Melo et al., 2025, Shahid et al., 2025, Petrone et al., 2026]. Vendor software support for the Panda, however, has been discontinued: current releases of franka_ros2 and libfranka target the newer Franka Research 3 (FR3) arm and recent ROS 2 distributions [Macenski et al., 2022], but no longer support the Panda [Franka Robotics, 2026]. Laboratories that rely on the Panda are therefore left on outdated, unmaintained software, an obstacle which matters most in collaborative applications, where the robot must be integrated with modern planning, perception and interaction tooling.

A second obstacle concerns position control. On the Panda, commanding joint positions or Cartesian poses through the external control interface is unreliable: the motion is prone to vibrations and to protective stops, to the point that existing frameworks discourage the position interface altogether [Škerlj et al., 2026b]. This is a serious limitation for collaborative use, since position commands are the natural output of, e.g., motion planners or perception-based modules, thus forcing researchers to put additional effort in devising a dedicated control architecture to execute such high-level commands. As we show in this work, the problem is not inherent to the robot, but to the specific implementation of the external control loop, and it can be resolved.

This work restores support for the Panda on ROS 2 Jazzy, a long-term support distribution, makes its position interface reliable, and releases the code as open source. Our contributions are:

  1. 1.

    An analysis of why external position control performs poorly on the Panda, tracing it to the timing of the control interface rather than to the robot itself (Sec. 2);

  2. 2.

    An asynchronous hardware interface that decouples the ros2_control loop from the robot’s real-time channel, together with a position-domain reference-generation scheme that makes the position interface reliable, and an optional rate-matching stage that enables slower command sources (Sec. 3);

  3. 3.

    The porting of franka_ros2 [Franka Robotics, 2025c] to ROS 2 Jazzy for the Panda, built on an extended and packaged libfranka driver which can run on a stock kernel without a real-time patch, both released as citable open-source repositories;

  4. 4.

    An experimental validation of the proposed reference-generation scheme (Sec. 4) and a demonstration in collaborative application scenarios at two experimental sites (Sec. 5).

1.1 Related Works

The reference software for Franka arms is the vendor franka_ros2 stack, built on ros2_control [Chitta et al., 2017]; its current releases require a libfranka version that supports only the FR3, leaving the Panda unsupported. The closest work to ours is multipanda_ros2 [Škerlj et al., 2026a], a ROS 2 framework for multi-robot control of Franka arms. It targets real-time torque control and multimanual coordination, with a MuJoCo-based simulation [Todorov et al., 2012] for bridging the sim-to-real gap, and it is implemented for the torque control mode only, explicitly leaving other modes as future work. Our goals are complementary: we focus on a current single-arm stack and, specifically, on making the position interface reliable, which multipanda_ros2 does not address.

1.2 Paper Structure

The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. Sec. 2 analyzes the Franka Control Interface (FCI) and its official ROS 2 implementation, and identifies the two mechanisms that make external position control fail. Sec. 3 presents the proposed architecture, and Sec. 4 validates it against the official one on the same robot and trajectory. Sec. 5 then demonstrates the stack on four applications chosen to span key capabilities for human-robot collaboration: planning and executing motions in a shared workspace, regulating the compliance the arm reacts to physical contact with, manipulating objects through position commands, and teleoperating the system through a haptic device. Each exercises a different command interface of the same hardware interface, and the first two are reproduced on two independent Panda instances. Lastly, Sec. 6 concludes the paper.

2 THE FCI AND ITS ROS 2 IMPLEMENTATION

2.1 FCI Communication Protocol

The FCI connects the robot’s onboard controller (INT in the following) to an external workstation (EXT) over UDP [Franka Robotics, 2025a]. Every Tδ≡1 msT_{\delta}\equiv$1\text{\,}\mathrm{ms}$, INT exchanges one packet pair with EXT, sending the current robot state and receiving the next command, and steps its internal controller [Franka Robotics, 2025a]. Two properties of this interface, illustrated in Fig. 1, are at the origin of the problem addressed in this work. First, libfranka exposes blocking reads only: the external process waits until a state packet arrives, so the EXT cycle is paced by INT. Second, when operating in external control mode, EXT must supply one reference sample for every INT cycle, since INT performs no onboard interpolation of sparse setpoints, unlike most industrial controllers. For a command to be applied at a given cycle, its round trip must fit within the cycle: the documentation requires the sum of the network round-trip time (RTT), the execution time of the external loop, and the INT’s processing time to stay below TδT_{\delta},

RTT+dEXT+dINT<Tδ,\mathrm{RTT}+d^{\mathrm{EXT}}+d^{\mathrm{INT}}\,<\,T_{\delta}, (1)

and in practice recommends keeping the external-loop contribution below dEXT<0.5 msd^{\mathrm{EXT}}<$0.5\text{\,}\mathrm{ms}$  [Franka Robotics, 2025a]. Whenever the budget of (1) is exceeded for a cycle, FCI discards that command; INT then holds the last commanded acceleration constant and keeps running, and only after 20 consecutive discarded commands does it stop the session with a communication error [Franka Robotics, 2025a]. This extrapolation lets the actual and commanded references drift apart during loss bursts.

2.2 Admissible References

Upon receiving a reference, INT reconstructs the kinematic quantities it was not given and verifies them against the robot’s limits. Let Δ\Delta denote the backward finite-difference operator,

Δ​𝐱≜𝐱⁡(k)−𝐱⁡(k−1),\Delta\mathbf{x}\triangleq\mathbf{x}(k)-\mathbf{x}(k-1),

with higher-order differences defined recursively as Δm​𝐱​(k)=Δ⁡(Δm−1​𝐱​(k))\Delta^{m}\mathbf{x}(k)=\Delta\bigl(\Delta^{m-1}\mathbf{x}(k)\bigr). For a joint position reference 𝐪s​(k)\mathbf{q}_{s}(k), the case analyzed in this work, the reconstruction reduces to

𝐪˙​(k)=Δ​𝐪s​(k)Tδ,𝐪¨​(k)=Δ​𝐪˙​(k)Tδ=Δ2​𝐪s​(k)Tδ2,𝐪˙˙˙​(k)=Δ​𝐪¨​(k)Tδ=Δ3​𝐪s​(k)Tδ3,\begin{split}\dot{\mathbf{q}}(k)&=\frac{\Delta\mathbf{q}_{s}(k)}{T_{\delta}},\\ \ddot{\mathbf{q}}(k)&=\frac{\Delta\dot{\mathbf{q}}(k)}{T_{\delta}}=\frac{\Delta^{2}\mathbf{q}_{s}(k)}{T_{\delta}^{2}},\\ \dddot{\mathbf{q}}(k)&=\frac{\Delta\ddot{\mathbf{q}}(k)}{T_{\delta}}=\frac{\Delta^{3}\mathbf{q}_{s}(k)}{T_{\delta}^{3}},\end{split} (2)

from which the required actuation torques follow through the rigid-body dynamics [Featherstone and Orin, 2008]

𝝉⁡(k)=𝐁⁡(𝐪⁡(k))​𝐪¨​(k)+𝐂⁡(𝐪⁡(k),𝐪˙​(k))​𝐪˙​(k)+𝐟⁡(𝐪˙​(k))+𝐠⁡(𝐪⁡(k)),\begin{split}\boldsymbol{\tau}(k)&=\mathbf{B}\bigl(\mathbf{q}(k)\bigr)\,\ddot{\mathbf{q}}(k)\\ &+\mathbf{C}\bigl(\mathbf{q}(k),\dot{\mathbf{q}}(k)\bigr)\,\dot{\mathbf{q}}(k)+\mathbf{f}\bigl(\dot{\mathbf{q}}(k)\bigr)+\mathbf{g}\bigl(\mathbf{q}(k)\bigr),\end{split} (3)

where 𝐁∈ℝn×n\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} is the inertia matrix, 𝐂∈ℝn×n\mathbf{C}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} accounts for the centrifugal and Coriolis effects, 𝐟∈ℝn\mathbf{f}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} contains joint friction, 𝐠∈ℝn\mathbf{g}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} collects the gravitational torques, and 𝐪,𝐪˙,𝐪¨∈ℝn\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}},\ddot{\mathbf{q}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} respectively represent actual joint positions, velocities, and accelerations, with n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} being the number of degrees of freedom11 1 n=7n=7 for the Panda robot.. INT verifies that positions, velocities, accelerations and jerks, as well as the torques in (3) and their rates, lie within their admissible ranges [Franka Robotics, 2025b]; a violation aborts the motion with a discontinuity or limit error. The admissible set of references is narrow. Since (2) divides successive differences by powers of TδT_{\delta}, a deviation ϵ\epsilon of 𝐪s​(k)\mathbf{q}_{s}(k) from the value that would preserve the previously established acceleration produces an additional jerk term of ϵ/Tδ3\epsilon/T_{\delta}^{3}. At Tδ=1 msT_{\delta}=$1\text{\,}\mathrm{ms}$, a deviation of a few microradians is enough to reach the jerk limit of the Panda [Franka Robotics, 2025b], and the other limits act analogously. Informally, we experimentally confirmed this microradian-scale tolerance: perturbing an otherwise feasible trajectory with uniform noise on the order of 1×10−6 rad1\text{\times}{10}^{-6}\text{\,}\mathrm{rad} was sufficient to trigger violations.

2.3 The Synchronous ROS 2 Implementation

The official franka_ros2 hardware interface performs the blocking FCI state read inside the read phase of the ros2_control main loop [Chitta et al., 2017]. The latter is driven by its own periodic thread: at every cycle, it wakes on a workstation timer, performs the read phase, the controllers’ updates and the write phase, then it sleeps until the next cycle boundary. Because the FCI read is blocking, the read phase itself does not complete until a new state packet arrives from INT. As a result, each iteration of the loop is paced by two different clocks: the beginning of the read phase is determined by the workstation timer (EXT), while its completion is determined by the arrival of the state packet generated by the robot controller (INT). Since INT and EXT’s clocks are independent, the relative phase between the two drifts slowly and leads to periodic unserved cycles.

Because the controllers execute between the read and the write, their computation lies on the critical path that (1) constrains. The immediate cost of this arrangement is visible in Table 1: the external ROS 2 control loop (RS) takes a median of 0.065 ms0.065\text{\,}\mathrm{ms}, against 0.012 ms0.012\text{\,}\mathrm{ms} for a bare libfranka program (LF) driving the same robot, and reaches 2.174 ms2.174\text{\,}\mathrm{ms} in the worst cycle, exceeding TδT_{\delta} and leading to the discard of the command of that cycle. It is worth highlighting that the controllers exercised for these measurements only forward joint position commands; critically, the margin is expected to shrink as the application becomes more demanding.

A more damaging consequence is produced by the drifting phase between the two clocks. When the EXT timer wakes shortly before receiving the next state packet from INT, the blocking read returns after a short wait and the cycle completes comfortably, producing a read-to-read interval close to TδT_{\delta} (Fig. 2, peak A). Conversely, when the EXT timer wakes immediately after a state packet has already been sent by INT, the read must wait almost a full period TδT_{\delta} for the following packet, since it returns only on a fresh state. This causes the ROS 2 cycle to overrun, and the next completed read will happen on a future wake of the EXT timer (as in Fig. 2, peaks B and C). When the EXT cycle overruns, one or more INT cycles remain unserved. During those cycles, INT holds the last commanded acceleration, as described in Sec. 2.1, thus distorting the intended reference. In our benchmarks (Table 1), RS results in 5.91 %5.91\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} unserved cycles, against 0.18 %0.18\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} for LF.

2.4 Reference Distortion under Sampling Jitter

Careful real-time configuration can reduce the number of unserved cycles, but a second effect survives it: on the cycles that are served, the reference itself is distorted by sampling jitter. In a typical ROS 2 deployment, a planned trajectory is sampled using the EXT workstation clock, which is typically a soft real-time machine communicating with INT through standard TCP/IP protocols. Network round trip, the non-deterministic latency of the operating-system network stack and scheduler on EXT, and the processing time of INT are all irreducible causes of sampling jitter [Reghenzani et al., 2019, Casini et al., 2019].

More formally, let 𝐪∗​(t)\mathbf{q}^{*}(t) be the planned trajectory, intended as a continuous function; the reference applied by INT at cycle kk is the trajectory evaluated by EXT at some instant ts​(k)t_{s}(k), i.e., 𝐪∗​(ts​(k))\mathbf{q}^{*}\bigl(t_{s}(k)\bigr), but (2) treats it as the uniform sample taken at k​TδkT_{\delta}. Even if the two clocks were perfectly aligned and INT were perfectly real-time, the jitter sources listed above would induce a time-domain sampling error of δ​t​(k)=ts​(k)−k​Tδ\delta t(k)=t_{s}(k)-kT_{\delta}. By first order Taylor expansion 𝐪s​(k)≈𝐪∗​(k​Tδ)+𝐪˙∗​(k​Tδ)​δ​t​(k)\mathbf{q}_{s}(k)\approx\mathbf{q}^{*}(kT_{\delta})+\dot{\mathbf{q}}^{*}(kT_{\delta})\delta t(k), therefore the sampling jitter induces an error in the finite differences calculated by INT. For the velocity,

𝐪˙​(k)=Δ​𝐪s​(k)Tδ≃Δ​𝐪∗​(k​Tδ)Tδ⏟intended velocity+𝐪˙∗​(k​Tδ)​Δ​δ​t​(k)Tδ⏟sampling error.\dot{\mathbf{q}}(k)=\frac{\Delta\mathbf{q}_{s}(k)}{T_{\delta}}\simeq\underbrace{\frac{\Delta\mathbf{q}^{*}(kT_{\delta})}{T_{\delta}}}_{\text{intended velocity}}+\underbrace{\dot{\mathbf{q}}^{*}(kT_{\delta})\frac{\Delta\delta t(k)}{T_{\delta}}}_{\text{sampling error}}. (4)

By chaining the finite differences of (2), the error induced by sampling jitter on the calculated jerk is 𝐪˙∗​Δ3​δ​t/Tδ3\dot{\mathbf{q}}^{*}\Delta^{3}\delta t/T_{\delta}^{3}. At q˙=1 rad/s\dot{q}=$1\text{\,}\mathrm{rad}\text{/}\mathrm{s}$, a single sample displaced by 4 µ​s4\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro s} displaces the commanded position by 4 µ​rad4\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro rad} and produces a jerk error of 1.2×104 rad/s31.2\text{\times}{10}^{4}\text{\,}\mathrm{rad}\text{/}{\mathrm{s}}^{3}, above the jerk limit of every joint of the robot [Franka Robotics, 2025b]. In the synchronous implementation, where the sample is taken as soon as the packet arrives, the problem is amplified as ts​(k)t_{s}(k) inherits the arrival jitter directly. This is shown in Fig. 3 and it explains why, in our tests, discontinuity aborts coincided with the cycles carrying the longest inter-arrival gaps.

Sampling the trajectory with INT’s own timestamps, i.e., the robot time carried by each state packet, removes this effect, and in our tests eliminated all violations; it requires, however, the trajectory in closed form and an external loop running exactly at INT’s rate, neither of which a controller-agnostic ROS 2 stack running on a general-purpose OS can assume.

To work around the problem, libfranka offers a rate limiter and a low-pass filter, but neither addresses its cause: the rate limiter only saturates the command derivatives to the admissible ranges, trading the discontinuity aborts for sustained link oscillations, while the low-pass filter attenuates the distortion without removing it, leaving audible motor noise and sporadic aborts.

2.5 Robustness of the Velocity and Torque Interfaces

The same jitter affects velocity and torque commands, yet these interfaces appear to work reliably, which explains why the problem has drawn little attention and why existing frameworks simply advise against the position interface [Škerlj et al., 2026a]. The reason follows from (2). Repeating the calculation of Sec. 2.4 for the velocity command interface, one obtains that the error induced on the calculated jerk is 𝐪¨∗​Δ2​δ​t/Tδ2\ddot{\mathbf{q}}^{*}\,\Delta^{2}\delta t/T_{\delta}^{2}: the sensitivity to the same timing error is reduced, making the position interface the most sensitive one. Another reason this problem is often unnoticed is that, when using the velocity or torque commands to control position, the loop closure itself absorbs the residual distortion as a disturbance. The scheme of Sec. 3.3 recovers both mechanisms within the position interface: the motion is driven by the commanded velocity, so that the increment reaching INT is not the difference of two displaced position samples, and the position command acts only through a loop closed on the robot’s own commanded state.

3 PROPOSED ARCHITECTURE

The proposed stack, summarized in Fig. 4, rests on two open-source components: a community-maintained libfranka repository [Tingelstad, 2024] that brings the modern control API to the Panda, extended with the Panda kinematic limits [Franka Robotics, 2025b], and a ROS 2 Jazzy package built on top of it providing a hardware interface for the robot [Franka Robotics, 2025c]. On this basis, Sec. 3.1 introduces the asynchronous communication thread that decouples the ros2_control loop from the FCI channel; Sec. 3.2 exploits this decoupling to run the ros2_control loop at a lower rate, matched to the robot loop by a rate matching stage applicable to any command interface; and Sec. 3.3 presents the position-domain reference generation that makes the position interface reliable.

3.1 Asynchronous Communication Thread

The asynchronous interface addresses the problem of Sec. 2.3 by confining FCI communication to a dedicated real-time thread, scheduled under SCHED_FIFO at the highest priority (99) and only containing the communication pipeline. The thread runs its own loop paced by the robot: each iteration blocks on the state read, publishes the received state into a mutex-protected buffer, fetches the next command from a second mutex-protected buffer, and transmits it within the budget of (1). On the ros2_control side, the logic reduces to buffer exchanges: the read phase copies the latest state and the write phase deposits the latest command. ROS-side jitter — being due to scheduling, DDS activity or controller cost — therefore terminates at the buffers and never reaches the FCI channel; conversely, a late ROS cycle no longer implies a missed robot cycle, since the thread keeps serving INT with a consistent command. The measurements of Table 1 quantify both effects: thanks to the dedicated thread, dEXTd^{\text{EXT}} has a median of 0.013 ms0.013\text{\,}\mathrm{ms}, comparable to the 0.012 ms0.012\text{\,}\mathrm{ms} of a bare libfranka program; the synchronous interface produces 5.91 %5.91\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} unserved cycles while our asynchronous implementation only produces 0.41 %0.41\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}. Furthermore, with the controllers moved off the real-time path, the delay added to the FCI exchange does not scale with the complexity of the application. In Fig. 2 the quantization of the synchronous interface gives way to the broad, continuous distribution of the bare libfranka loop: the thread is paced by the arrival of the packets rather than by a workstation timer, and the phase competition of Sec. 2.3 does not arise.

Robustness to packet loss is handled at the same level. The thread timestamps every state read and compares the measured inter-arrival period T^​(k)\hat{T}(k) against TδT_{\delta}; whenever |T^​(k)−Tδ|>0.25 ms|\hat{T}(k)-T_{\delta}|>$0.25\text{\,}\mathrm{ms}$, the cycle is flagged as anomalous, the write is skipped, and the last consistent command is held, preventing a command computed against a stale or duplicated state from being differentiated by (2). Position-type modes are additionally gated at activation: no command is transmitted until both the thread and the ROS-side loop have consumed a fresh state, avoiding first-cycle steps at controller switches.

Because the timing requirement is confined to the communication thread, and the processing in the latter is reduced to a bare minimum, the stack does not enforce the use of a real-time kernel patch: the experiments of Sec. 4 were obtained on a stock kernel with SCHED_FIFO scheduling alone.

3.2 Rate Matching for Slower Control Loops

The proposed architecture admits control loops slower than what FCI prescribes: the ros2_control loop may run at any rate fEXT≤fINTf_{\text{EXT}}\leq f_{\text{INT}}, which relaxes its real-time requirements and matches the native rate of most command sources, from motion planners to teleoperation devices. The rate-matching stage described here is what makes this possible.

A source running at fEXTf_{\text{EXT}} delivers one update every N=⌈fINT/fEXT⌉N=\lceil f_{\text{INT}}/f_{\text{EXT}}\rceil robot cycles. Passing those command updates on as they arrive would hold each value for N−1N-1 cycles and step on the NN-th, and (2) would turn that staircase into impulsive motor actions. To prevent this, a rate-matching moving-average filter is run on the communication thread to smooth the reference without distorting it. By choosing the window of the filter as N=⌈fINT/fEXT⌉N=\lceil f_{\text{INT}}/f_{\text{EXT}}\rceil, each command update is distributed across the NN cycles separating it from the next, and the staircase becomes a piecewise-linear ramp. The filter introduces a group delay of N−12Tδ=(N−1)×\frac{N-1}{2}T_{\delta}=(N-1)\times0.5 ms0.5\text{\,}\mathrm{ms}. The delay is limited to a few milliseconds assuming a reasonable value of fEXT≥100 Hzf_{\text{EXT}}\geq$100\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz}$. Because it acts on the command samples irrespective of their meaning, the filter applies to any command interface.

3.3 Position-Domain Reference Generation

The analysis of Sec. 2.4 indicates that any scheme sampling the trajectory with the workstation clock inherits sampling jitter and, over time, clock drift. As a consequence, the proposed control scheme abandons external time references and recovers the two mechanisms that make the velocity and torque interfaces robust (Sec. 2.5).

Let 𝐪d​(k)\mathbf{q}_{d}(k) be the last commanded position reported by INT in the state packet; 𝐪ext​(k)\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{ext}}(k) be the position command (raw or filtered) most recently deposited by the ROS side and 𝐪˙ext​(k)\dot{\mathbf{q}}_{\mathrm{ext}}(k) be its feed-forward velocity obtained by finite-differencing successive position commands. The proposed method generates the reference in the position domain from the latest available position command

𝐪s​(k)=𝐪d​(k)+Tδ​𝐪˙ext​(k)+λ⁡(𝐪ext​(k)−𝐪d​(k)),\mathbf{q}_{s}(k)\,=\,\mathbf{q}_{d}(k)+T_{\delta}\,\dot{\mathbf{q}}_{\mathrm{ext}}(k)+\lambda\bigl(\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{ext}}(k)-\mathbf{q}_{d}(k)\bigr), (5)

where λ\lambda is a tunable parameter.

Equation (5) has three properties that address the failure modes of Sec. 2: (i) the motion is driven by the feed-forward term Tδ​𝐪˙ext​(k)T_{\delta}\dot{\mathbf{q}}_{\mathrm{ext}}(k) while the position enters only through a proportional term closing the loop on 𝐪d​(k)\mathbf{q}_{d}(k), so the position inherits the sensitivity of the velocity interface; (ii) if the external stream stalls, the reference degrades gracefully toward the last target instead of stepping; (iii) no timestamp of either machine appears in it, making it immune to clock drift.

An analogous scheme covers the Cartesian pose interface: the commanded pose is propagated by the externally commanded twist over one period, and a proportional twist correction toward the externally commanded pose is applied incrementally.

Since the scheme already delivers a continuous command stream, the command low-pass filter offered by libfranka is redundant, and it must in fact be disabled: applied to an incremental command it scales the increment itself, and with it both the feed-forward term and the correction gain, so that the robot follows a fraction of the commanded motion (Sec. 4).

We do not claim formal guarantees for the proposed scheme; its behavior is assessed empirically in our experiments.

4 EXPERIMENTAL VALIDATION

4.1 Setup

All experiments run on a Panda controlled from a workstation running Ubuntu 24.04 (patched with PREEMPT_RT [Reghenzani et al., 2019]) and ROS 2 Jazzy, connected to the robot by a dedicated Ethernet link. We compare the official (synchronous) franka_ros2 hardware interface ported to ROS 2 Jazzy with our asynchronous interface.

Joint trajectories are produced by a robot-agnostic reference generator [Risi et al., 2026], which validates and interpolates the waypoints and publishes the resulting command stream to the controller under test. The same ∼18.32 s\sim$18.32\text{\,}\mathrm{s}$ multi-joint trajectory is replayed in every run.

Loop timings are collected with LTTng user-space tracepoints placed around the state read and the command write, as reported in Sec. 2.3 and Sec. 3.1; robot states and the trajectory results of each run are recorded from the ROS 2 graph.

4.2 Position Control

We evaluate the performance of the proposed position reference generation scheme in (5) by comparing executions of the same trajectory with both the synchronous and asynchronous interfaces. For the synchronous interface, the low-pass filter is active as it is required to safely control the arm via position commands. For the asynchronous interface, we compare the behavior with and without the low-pass filter and set the control frequency to fEXT=fINT=1 kHzf_{\text{EXT}}=f_{\text{INT}}=$1\text{\,}\mathrm{kHz}$. All three configurations have the rate limiter enabled to prevent communication errors. For the experiments we set λ=1×10−3\lambda=$1\text{\times}{10}^{-3}$.

Fig. 5 compares the measured joint velocity and its spectrum for three configurations: synchronous, the proposed asynchronous configuration, and the proposed one with the addition of the low-pass filter. The synchronous interface follows the reference but carries an order of magnitude more spectral power than the other two configurations in the 20−15020-150 Hz band: this is the roughness the rate limiter leaves behind once it has removed the invalid commands, and it manifests as motor noise during the execution of the trajectory. The low-pass filter suppresses that excess but, as discussed in Sec. 3.3, it hinders the tracking by scaling the incremental command (visible as the shrunken joint velocity curve in Fig. 5). The proposed configuration attains faithful tracking while keeping the low band power of the filtered case. The remaining joints behave consistently22 2 Results for all joints are available at https://sites.google.com/view/fer-ros2/results.

4.3 Rate Matching

To validate the rate matching mechanism described in Sec. 3.2, the robot is driven from a velocity command source running at fEXT=125 Hzf_{\text{EXT}}=$125\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz}$ (hence N=8N=8) and we measure what reaches the robot with the rate-matching stage enabled and disabled.

Results are shown in Fig. 6: with the stage disabled, the command is the zero-order hold of the source, constant for N−1N-1 cycles and stepping on the NN-th; the single step carries the whole update, so the per-cycle increment presented to INT is NN times the intended one. With the stage enabled, the same update is spread across the NN cycles it spans and the command becomes a ramp whose per-cycle increment is the intended one, at the analytical cost of a group delay of N−12​Tδ=3.5 ms\frac{N-1}{2}T_{\delta}=$3.5\text{\,}\mathrm{ms}$.

5 APPLICATIONS

We demonstrate the proposed stack on four applications, each exercising a capability that collaborative robotics commonly relies on:

  1. 1.

    collision-aware motion planning and execution via MoveIt! and ROS2-native controllers (Sec. 5.1);

  2. 2.

    compliance control for physical human-robot interaction, at standstill and along trajectories, with and without human perturbation (Sec. 5.2);

  3. 3.

    an end-to-end, position-controlled pick-and-place (Sec. 5.3);

  4. 4.

    haptic teleoperation of a mobile manipulator (Sec. 5.4).

Together they exercise the position, velocity and torque command interfaces of our hardware interface. The MoveIt! planning and compliance control applications were run on two different Panda setups, hosted in two different institutions, hereinafter referred to as Lab A and Lab B33 3 The labs’ names will be disclosed together with the authors’ names in case of acceptance., while pick-and-place and teleoperation were run in Lab A only, showing that the same software runs unchanged across different setups and machines. Moreover, to ease the shake-out of the system for new users, we have restored all the basic libfranka examples44 4 https://anonymous.4open.science/r/libfranka-636F which, for the sake of brevity, are shown on our website55 5 https://sites.google.com/view/fer-ros2/libfranka. It is worth highlighting that, in Lab A, the applications are run with a non-realtime kernel, to demonstrate that, as mentioned in Sec. 3.1, patching the system with PREEMPT_RT is not a strict requirement as it was for the official release of libfranka.

5.1 MoveIt! planning and execution

This application exercises the MoveIt! planning and execution pipeline (Fig. 7). Starting from the initial configuration (Fig. 7(a)), the robot plans a motion to a randomly sampled goal pose (Fig. 7(b)) and executes it (Fig. 7(c)) through an effort-based joint_trajectory_controller tuned with the PID gains of Table 2. This confirms that the stack effortlessly integrates with the standard ROS 2 planning tools, letting users move the robot to any feasible desired pose defined by the target application.

5.2 Compliance control

This application deploys a custom torque controller, named the compliance controller, which applies a Cartesian-space PD control law at the end-effector, whose gains set how compliant the arm is to human interaction:

𝝉=𝐉⊤​(𝐪)​(𝐊P​𝐱~+𝐊D​𝐱~˙)+𝐂⁡(𝐪,𝐪˙)​𝐪˙+𝐟⁡(𝐪˙)+𝐠⁡(𝐪)+(𝐈n−𝐉⊤​(𝐪)​𝐉†​(𝐪))​(k0​(𝐪0−𝐪)−2​k0​𝐪˙)\begin{split}\boldsymbol{\tau}&=\mathbf{J}^{\top}(\mathbf{q})(\mathbf{K}_{P}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}+\mathbf{K}_{D}\dot{\tilde{\mathbf{x}}})+\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}})\dot{\mathbf{q}}+\mathbf{f}(\dot{\mathbf{q}})+\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{q})\\ &+\bigl(\mathbf{I}_{n}-\mathbf{J}^{\top}(\mathbf{q})\mathbf{J}^{\dagger}(\mathbf{q})\bigr)\bigl(k_{0}(\mathbf{q}_{0}-\mathbf{q})-2\sqrt{k_{0}}\dot{\mathbf{q}}\bigr)\end{split} (6)

where 𝐱\mathbf{x} and 𝐱˙\dot{\mathbf{x}} are the end-effector pose and twist, ∙~≜∙d−∙\tilde{\bullet}\triangleq\bullet_{d}-\bullet indicates the error, and ∙d\bullet_{d} represents the desired quantity. 𝐈n\mathbf{I}_{n} is the n×nn\times n identity matrix, and 𝐉⁡(𝐪)∈ℝ6×n\mathbf{J}(\mathbf{q})\in\mathbb{R}^{6\times n} is the configuration-dependent Jacobian matrix, with †\dagger indicating the pseudo-inverse of its transpose, while k0≔1.0k_{0}\coloneqq 1.0 and 𝐪0≔[0,0,0,−90 °,0,107 °,0]⊤\mathbf{q}_{0}\coloneqq[0,0,0,$-90\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree}$,0,$107\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree}$,0]^{\top} are the nullspace stiffness and setpoint, respectively.

We exercise this controller in four different setups, with control gains 𝐊P\mathbf{K}_{P} and 𝐊D\mathbf{K}_{D} set according to Table 2:

  1. A)

    standstill human perturbation with stiff behavior;

  2. B)

    standstill human perturbation with compliant behavior;

  3. C)

    trajectory tracking with stiff behavior;

  4. D)

    trajectory tracking with compliant behavior and human perturbation.

By retuning the Cartesian gains 𝐊P\mathbf{K}_{P} and 𝐊D\mathbf{K}_{D} as in Table 2, the controller ranges from stiff to compliant behavior. With stiff gains, the arm holds its pose or tracks its trajectory tightly and resists contact; with compliant gains, it yields to external forces. Fig. 8 shows both regimes: at standstill (top), the robot reacts softly to a human push under compliant gains while staying firm under stiff ones; along a trajectory (bottom), the human can deflect the compliant robot, whereas the stiff run is executed without human contact for safety (2C) and tracks unperturbed. Readers are invited to see the full videos for a better visualization of these behaviors66 6 https://sites.google.com/view/fer-ros2/applications/compliance-control.

5.3 Pick-and-place

This application runs a complete pick-and-place task through the position command interface, the interface discouraged on the Panda by [Škerlj et al., 2026a] and made reliable by this work. We adopt a second custom controller, the Cartesian pose controller, defined by:

𝐪˙c=(𝐉⊤​(𝐪)​𝐉​(𝐪)+α​𝐈n)−1​𝐉⊤​(𝐪)​(𝐊P​𝐱~+𝐱˙d),𝐪c=∫t𝐪˙c​dt,\begin{split}\dot{\mathbf{q}}_{c}&=\bigl(\mathbf{J}^{\top}(\mathbf{q})\mathbf{J}(\mathbf{q})+\alpha\mathbf{I}_{n}\bigr)^{-1}\mathbf{J}^{\top}(\mathbf{q})(\mathbf{K}_{P}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}+\dot{\mathbf{x}}_{d}),\\ \mathbf{q}_{c}&=\int_{t}{\dot{\mathbf{q}}_{c}dt},\end{split} (7)

with 𝐊P\mathbf{K}_{P} set as in Table 2 and α≔1×10−6\alpha\coloneqq$1\text{\times}{10}^{-6}$. Notably, this controller claims the position command interfaces directly by commanding 𝐪c\mathbf{q}_{c}, thus exercising the interface this work makes reliable.

The robot grasps an object from one surface and places it, re-oriented, on another at a different height. Fig. 9 illustrates the procedure, pairing snapshots of the real execution (top) with the MoveIt! planning requests computed through its C++ API and previewed to the user in RViz (bottom).

5.4 Teleoperation

A human operator teleoperates the system through a haptic device, whose motion is mapped either to Cartesian-space references (𝐱d\mathbf{x}_{d} in (6)) for the arm or to twist commands for a Husky A200 mobile base, alternating between the two. The arm tracks these references with the compliance controller (6), using the gains of Table 2 and k0≔0.3k_{0}\coloneqq 0.3. The task is similar to the pick-and-place of Sec. 5.3, but the mobile base extends the arm’s workspace: as Fig. 10 shows, it carries the manipulator to objects beyond its fixed reach, which it then grasps and releases at new locations.

6 CONCLUSIONS

This work brings the Franka Emika Panda back onto a current ROS 2 stack and makes its position command interface usable. As a preliminary analysis, we traced the failure of external position control to the timing of the control loop rather than to the robot. In the official implementation, the external workstation timer triggers the blocking FCI read, but the robot’s controller dictates when new data arrives. We concluded that, as these two clocks are independent, their relative phase drifts, causing periodic delays that leave robot cycles unserved and make the external computer distort the command stream by sampling the trajectory at instants whose jitter the onboard motion generator reads as spurious velocity and jerk.

To address this issue, the proposed architecture separates the two concerns. A real-time thread owns the communication with the robot and keeps the external loop within the interface budget, at a cost indistinguishable from a bare libfranka program, while the ros2_control loop is free to run at its own rate, matched to the robot’s by a filtering stage. References are generated in the position domain, anchored to the robot’s own commanded state, so no clock of the workstation enters the command. The position interface then tracks as accurately as the synchronous one while reducing the spectral content that the rate limiter leaves behind, and the four applications of Sec. 5 exercise the position, velocity and torque interfaces on two independent setups. Both repositories are released as open source.

The approach has limits that are worth stating. The reference generation is assessed empirically: we make no formal claim on the smoothness or the stability of the resulting command stream, and the gain λ\lambda trades the speed at which the robot’s state rejoins the external reference against the size of the per-cycle correction. The rate-matching stage costs a group delay that grows with the ratio of the two rates, which bounds how slowly the ROS side can usefully run. Unserved cycles are reduced but not removed, since a general-purpose workstation retains a residual scheduling latency of its own.

Future work follows these limits. A correction saturated at the admissible per-cycle increment would replace the fixed gain and reconcile the two states at the fastest feasible rate, which also opens the way to the constraint-aware reference generation needed under sustained packet loss. The stack will be ported to the next ROS 2 distribution, and the position-domain scheme, which assumes nothing specific to this robot beyond the structure of its command interface, is a candidate for other manipulators whose controllers expose a commanded state.
